messages.content:
You are proposing scientific conjectures. A conjecture is a bold, specific,
falsifiable claim or approach -- not a summary, not a plan, and not a hedge.
Write plainly.

Why do long-running software systems become harder to change over time, even when every individual change was reviewed, tested, and locally correct?

Stay within this direction: Entropy increase in the space of reachable configurations relative to explicit constraints

Generate 10 candidate conjectures within that direction, sampled from the
full distribution of responses you could give. For each, give the
conjecture and your estimated probability that it is the response you would
give to this prompt. Every candidate's probability must be below 0.10.
Output exactly one JSON object and nothing else:
{"candidates": [{"conjecture": "<2-4 sentences>", "probability": <number below 0.10>}, ... 10 items]}

message.content: {"candidates": [{"conjecture": "Each locally correct change expands the set of reachable configurations faster than it expands the set of explicitly tested configurations, so the fraction of the reachable space covered by constraints monotonically decreases. The system becomes harder to change not because any single change introduced a defect, but because the ratio of unconstrained reachable states to constrained ones grows asymptotically toward one.", "probability": 0.09}, {"conjecture": "Test suites constrain only the specific configurations exercised, so each passing change certificates a finite slice of behavior while the interaction surface among components grows combinatorially. The entropy increase is the divergence between the reachable configuration space (growing exponentially via feature interaction) and the constraint space (growing only linearly via added test cases).", "probability": 0.08}, {"conjecture": "Implicit invariants—unstated assumptions about unreachable configurations that hold at initial low entropy—are never encoded as explicit constraints because they never fail. Each locally correct change silently expands the reachable configuration space until it intersects a phantom invariant, at which point the system has high entropy relative to zero explicit constraints guarding that invariant, making the failure appear sudden and the change appear risky.", "probability": 0.07}, {"conjecture": "Every locally correct change is accepted because it satisfies all explicit constraints, but it simultaneously creates new reachable configurations that no existing constraint covers. The accumulation of these unconstrained reachable states constitutes a growing implicit debt that makes future changes harder because the probability of disturbing an unconstrained-but-load-bearing configuration increases monotonically with the entropy of the reachable space.", "probability": 0.07}, {"conjecture": "Code review and testing are entropy-minimizing operations over the delta being changed but entropy-maximizing over the system as a whole, because they certify that the new state satisfies local constraints while the new state itself increases the total number of reachable configurations. The system degrades because local correctness is an entropy-increasing operation globally: it expands the reachable space without proportionally expanding the constraint space.", "probability": 0.06}, {"conjecture": "Long-running systems accumulate configuration-space entropy because each change adds new dimensions to the reachable space (new flags, states, paths) while constraints remain anchored to historically observed configurations. The difficulty of change scales with the Shannon entropy of the reachable configuration distribution minus the Shannon entropy of the constrained configuration distribution, which grows because the former acquires new support faster than the latter.", "probability": 0.06}, {"conjecture": "The fundamental problem is that explicit constraints can only be added retroactively after a failure is observed, but each change adds reachable configurations that have never been observed. The system becomes harder to change because the fraction of its reachable configuration space that has ever been traversed— and thus constrained—approaches zero as the system grows, leaving an increasing majority of the reachable space unconstrained and thus increasingly likely to be disturbed by any change.", "probability": 0.05}, {"conjecture": "Refactoring reduces entropy in the implementation space but increases entropy in the configuration space by creating new transitional states and paths, and since tests constrain configurations not implementations, every refactor that passes tests has increased the entropy of reachable configurations relative to constraints. Long-running systems are harder to change because they have been refactored enough times that their reachable configuration space entropy vastly exceeds their constraint entropy.", "probability": 0.05}, {"conjecture": "The constraint set of a long-running system forms a sparse, incomplete graph over the reachable configuration space, and each accepted change adds nodes to the configuration space faster than the review process adds edges to the constraint graph. The increasing difficulty of change is the increasing graph diameter between any new change and its nearest explicit constraint, which grows as the reachable space expands faster than the constraint graph densifies.", "probability": 0.04}, {"conjecture": "Long-running systems become harder to change because the set of reachable configurations drifts away from the set of explicitly constrained configurations at a rate proportional to the number of accepted changes, since each change is validated against existing constraints but creates configurations those constraints were never designed to cover. The system's changeability is inversely related to the KL-divergence between the distribution of reachable configurations and the distribution of constrained configurations, which increases monotonically because constraints are stationary while reachability grows.", "probability": 0.04}]}
